summary.note: Counted from the rows below, and consistent with them: every `gaps` row has at least one entry in `findings`, every `faithful` row has none. Re-deriving the ten rows against upstream v1.102.3 moved #299 from `faithful` to `gaps` - the backlog prose it rewrote still credits Go's `tailscale up` with `--nickname` - and wrote up two more divergences under #293, so this edition states four faithful, six gaps and nine findings where the first one stated five, five and seven.

auditedPrs.notes: The refusal ORDER of runServeCombined, zero-is-unset ports, --tun as serveTypeTUN, the acceptAppCapsFlag grammar and --bg=false all match serve_v2.go at the pin. Three strings from the same two functions do not: the too-high-port refusal is absent, both --service refusals lost Go's literal 'Error: ' prefix, and the multiple-types refusal gained a trailing hint.

The --exit-node-allow-lan-access refusal is verbatim prefsFromUpArgs (up.go:305-307) and correctly scoped to up only. The --nickname rename matches setProfilePrefs for a non-empty name; the empty-name arm diverges (Go's else branch restores the login name).

updateKubeconfig, appendOrSetNamed, the KUBECONFIG walk, the 0600 write and the two-way Service lookup match configure-kube.go. Two error paths do not come across: Go's os.MkdirAll was narrowed to a one-level create (and miscited in a code comment as os.Mkdir), and checkKubeconfigWritable has no analogue.

Purely fork-internal failure ordering: a failed profiles.json rename no longer short-circuits the engine reconcile. Go has no separable rename step to diverge from - profileManager.SetPrefs writes prefs and the login profile through one path - and no success-path behaviour, message or flag moves.

The added test drives the real built tnet binary and its assertions are correct. The backlog prose it rewrote is not: it still opens by crediting Go's `tailscale up` with --nickname, which up.go registers only under `if cmd == "login"`. --auth-key, --login-server and the hidden --host-routes are on up as claimed.

`switch remove` on the current profile is now Go's exit-0 'already on account' no-op, ordered ahead of the fork's default-profile refusal, and name matching now takes the first hit as matchProfile does. The bigger divergence in the same file is untouched: `switch <unmatched>` creates a profile where Go refuses.

Checked against cmd/tailscaled/tailscaled.go at the pin: the flag is declared (line 222), the empty-path carve-out matches `args.birdSocketPath != ""` (line 290), and the refusal precedes the --cleanup exit (290 vs 520), as ported. Exit 1 on stderr matches log.SetFlags(0)+log.Fatalf. The reworded reason is a stated departure.

Verb sets, the accepted bare parent, the 'unsupported command:' opening and the requiresStandalone/requiresGUI split all match configure_apple.go. Naming the refused verb, appending a pointer to `tnet install` and registering on Linux are declared departures; the out-of-scope ruling matches how Go gates the other six commands.

Matches runFileGetOneBatch: the moved tally goes to errs when the drain cleared nothing from a non-empty inbox and to the verbose line otherwise, never both, and runFileGet's split (all but the last error to stdout, the last returned) is reproduced. The compact per-file progress line is a pre-existing fork addition, documented in place.

Argument-count-before-flag ordering, `unknown network <net>`, the family filter's 'address <host>: no suitable address found' and the IP-literal short circuit all match runDebugResolve and the resolver it calls. The empty-hostname message does not.

gate.detail: Run on main at 674df0d with CARGO_BUILD_JOBS=4, RUST_TEST_THREADS=4, TS_RS_EXPERIMENT=this_is_unstable_software, RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN=1.95.0 (no default toolchain is configured on this box, so the pin has to be named). cargo fmt --all --check: exit 0. cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings: exit 0. cargo test --all-targets: exit 0, 837 tests passed across 28 targets, 0 failed. cargo build --release --bins: exit 0.

findings.title: A switch target matching no profile is created instead of refused
findings.detail: Go's switchProfile calls matchProfile and, on a miss, prints `No profile named %q` and exits 1; it never creates a profile. The merged Backend::switch_profile falls through a resolver miss to `None if profile::is_valid_profile_id(target) => target` (src/ipn/mod.rs:1884) and treats the unmatched string as a NEW profile id: it tears down the live device, registers the id in profiles.json, repoints the current-profile pointer and comes up on empty prefs. So a mistyped `tnet switch wrok-laptop` disconnects the node into a fresh empty profile where `tailscale switch wrok-laptop` refuses and leaves the session alone. PR #301 fixed the adjacent tie case in resolve_target_to_id and names this hazard in its own commit body, but left the create-on-miss path in place.

findings.title: The rewritten backlog entry still credits Go's `up` with --nickname, which only `login` has
findings.detail: newUpFlagSet registers the nickname flag inside `if cmd == "login" { upf.StringVar(&upArgs.profileName, "nickname", ...) }` (up.go:136-138), so `tailscale up --nickname X` is itself a flag-parse error upstream; only `tailscale login --nickname` exists. The entry PR #299 rewrote still opens with "Go's `tailscale up` takes `--auth-key` ..., `--login-server`, `--nickname` and the hidden `--host-routes`" and then prescribes `up --nickname` as new `up` behaviour "that has to do what `set --nickname` does". Correcting exactly this sentence was the whole point of the change, and it directs an implementer to add a flag upstream's `up` does not have - which would then make `tnet up` diverge in the other direction. The other three are registered on up as claimed (auth-key at up.go:102, login-server at 108, host-routes at 111), and the test the PR added asserts the correct current behaviour, so the defect is confined to the prose.

findings.title: The kubeconfig parent directory is created one level deep where Go creates the whole tree
findings.detail: setKubeconfigForPeer stats the target's parent and, when it does not exist, calls `os.MkdirAll(dir, 0755)` wrapped in kubeconfigAccessErr - so `KUBECONFIG=/var/tmp/a/b/config tailscale configure kubeconfig <peer>` creates a/b and writes the file. The merged set_kubeconfig_for_peer uses a single std::fs::DirBuilder::create (src/bin/tnet.rs:13582), and the comment above it cites Go as `os.Mkdir(dir, 0755)` - "one level, not MkdirAll". Against the pinned ref that citation is the wrong way round, and the same command line fails here with a creation error where Go succeeds.

findings.title: Go's checkKubeconfigWritable precheck was not ported, so an unwritable kubeconfig fails late and in other words
findings.detail: runConfigureKubeconfig calls `checkKubeconfigWritable(kubeconfig)` once the peer FQDN is resolved and before setKubeconfigForPeer touches anything, returning kubeconfigAccessErr (`cannot write kubeconfig at %q: %w`) with extra guidance for a sandboxed macOS GUI build. The merged run_configure_kubeconfig has no equivalent - nothing in src/bin/tnet.rs matches `cannot write kubeconfig`. The port discovers the problem only by acting, so an unwritable target surfaces as whichever step fails first, the last of them only after the merge has already been computed. Both refuse and neither writes a partial file, so this is a message-and-ordering divergence rather than lost data.

findings.title: Go's too-high serve port refusal was dropped from the ported srvTypeAndPortFromFlags
findings.detail: srvTypeAndPortFromFlags reads the four listener flags as plain uints and refuses an out-of-range one itself: `if v > math.MaxUint16 { return 0, 0, fmt.Errorf("port number %d is too high for %s flag", v, srvType) }` (serve_v2.go:1407), which runServeCombined reports as the command's error with exit 1. The merged ServeFlags types https/http/tcp/tls_terminated_tcp as Option<u16> (src/bin/tnet.rs:1630-1642), so `tnet serve --https=70000 3000` dies in clap with "invalid value ... is not in 0..=65535" and exit 2 before serve_kind_and_port runs. The same diff ported the zero-is-unset and multiple-types rules out of that one function and widened --proxy-protocol to u64 for exactly this reason, so the omission is inconsistent with its own approach; the commit body rejects it on the grounds that clap refuses anyway, which changes both the message and the exit status.

findings.title: Both --service refusals drop Go's literal 'Error: ' prefix
findings.detail: runServeCombined returns `errors.New("Error: --service flag is not supported with funnel")` (serve_v2.go:405) and `errors.New("Error: --service flag is only compatible with background mode")` (serve_v2.go:416) - the prefix is part of the string upstream, not something a printer adds. check_serve_flags bails with those two lines minus the prefix (src/bin/tnet.rs:12428 and 12431) while the commit body states the refusals land in Go's words. The two neighbouring refusals it ported alongside them, for --proxy-protocol and --tun, carry no prefix upstream and none here, so the divergence is specific to these two. A script matching upstream's stderr exactly does not match.

findings.title: The ported multiple-types refusal appends a hint Go does not print
findings.detail: srvTypeAndPortFromFlags refuses with exactly `cannot serve multiple types for a single mount point` and nothing else. The merged serve_kind_and_port bails with that sentence plus ": give exactly one of --https / --http / --tcp / --tls-terminated-tcp / --tun (they name the same listener)" (src/bin/tnet.rs), while the commit body presents the check as landing "with Go's 'cannot serve multiple types for a single mount point'". The added clause is helpful but it is not upstream's line, so the same stderr-matching script that the 'Error: ' prefix finding breaks also breaks here, and the commit's own claim of verbatim wording does not hold for the one message it names.

findings.title: An empty hostname reports the wrong resolver error
findings.detail: runDebugResolve hands args[0] straight to net.DefaultResolver.LookupIP (debug.go:1423) after only the argument-count check, so the empty-host case is decided by Go's stdlib guard, which returns a DNSError carrying errNoSuchHost - rendered `lookup : no such host`. The merged resolve_lookup bails with `lookup : no suitable address found` (src/bin/tnet.rs), which is the string LookupIP uses for the different case where the family filter empties a non-empty result, and the code comment above it asserts Go's guard is `&DNSError{Err: "no suitable address found", Name: ""}`. The two upstream failures become indistinguishable: "you gave me no name" now reads as "that name has no address of the family you asked for", which is the message the same port emits, correctly, one branch away.
findings.upstream: cmd/tailscale/cli/debug.go @ 53a0d659afa51835dd7a9283873cca44261454f8 (runDebugResolve, whose only lookup path is net.DefaultResolver.LookupIP)

findings.title: An empty --nickname blanks the profile display name where Go restores the login name
findings.detail: setProfilePrefs is an if/else, not a guarded set: `if prefsIn.ProfileName() != "" { lp.Name = prefsIn.ProfileName() } else { lp.Name = up.LoginName }`. Go therefore never leaves a profile with a blank Name - clearing the nickname puts the account's login name back, which is what `switch --list` prints in its Account column and what matchProfile's third pass resolves against. The merged begin_set calls rename_current_profile(name.as_deref().unwrap_or("")), storing an empty name, and both readers then fall back to the profile id. So after `tnet set --nickname=` the profile is addressable only by id where Go leaves it addressable by login name. The commit body acknowledges the fallback differs; the daemon holds no login name to substitute, so closing this needs that value tracked first.
